specPoints.text: understand that the effect of temperature on the position of equilibrium is explained using a change in the value of the equilibrium constant

primer.text: Disturb an equilibrium and it pushes back. This note arms you with Le Chatelier's principle across all three levers - concentration, pressure and temperature - with the gas-mole census for pressure questions and the endothermic compass for heat, right down to the equal-moles case where nothing moves.

lessons.title: Position of equilibrium and the counteracting principle
lessons.opening: Equilibrium has an address: left means reactant-rich, right means product-rich. Le Chatelier's principle is the navigation rule - disturb the system and it moves to soften the disturbance, shifting concentration, pressure or temperature.
keyPoints: The position of equilibrium describes how the product and reactant amounts balance in the mixture.
Shifting left raises reactant concentration; shifting right raises product concentration.
Le Chatelier's principle: a change to a system at equilibrium moves the position to counteract the change.
The principle predicts shifts for changes in concentration, pressure and temperature.

low.restatement: The equilibrium's 'position' is where the mixture's balance sits; any imposed change is answered by a shift that partially undoes it.
low.analogy: A see-saw with an automatic rider: add weight to one side and the rider slides that way to restore balance.
low.examPointer: Answer format: state the shift direction, then say which side's concentration rises as a result.

medium.restatement: Counteraction is partial, never complete: the system reduces the imposed change but cannot erase it. The three levers - concentration, pressure, temperature - each map onto a specific directional response.
medium.analogy: A thermostat that cools when you heat the room: it dampens your change without reversing it.
medium.examPointer: Name all three levers when the question asks 'when is the principle used to predict shifts'.

check.stem: The position of equilibrium refers to

options.text: How the product and reactant amounts balance in the mixture
options.explanation: Position is a composition statement, not a rate statement.

options.text: The rate of the forward reaction
options.explanation: Rates are equal at equilibrium regardless of position.

options.text: The time taken to reach equilibrium
options.explanation: Time to equilibrium is a kinetics question, not position.

options.text: The total pressure of the vessel
options.explanation: Pressure is a condition, not the position itself.

check.stem: A shift to the right means

options.text: The concentration of products increases
options.explanation: Rightward shift builds the product side of the equation.

options.text: The concentration of reactants increases
options.explanation: That is a leftward shift.

options.text: Both concentrations fall to zero
options.explanation: Equilibrium mixtures never empty out.

options.text: The rate of the backward reaction rises above the forward
options.explanation: A rightward shift corresponds to forward outrunning backward until a new balance.

check.stem: Le Chatelier's principle says that when a disturbance hits a system at equilibrium,

options.text: The position of equilibrium moves to counteract the change
options.explanation: Counteraction is the defining response of the principle.

options.text: The reaction stops until the change is removed
options.explanation: Equilibria respond, they do not pause.

options.text: The position moves to amplify the change
options.explanation: Amplification is the opposite of the principle.

options.text: Only temperature changes can shift the position
options.explanation: Concentration and pressure also shift equilibria.

check.stem: Which three variables does the principle predict shifts for?

options.text: Concentration, pressure and temperature
options.explanation: These are the three disturbance classes the principle covers.

options.text: Catalyst amount, volume of vessel and colour
options.explanation: Catalysts shift nothing; colour is an observation.

options.text: Mass, molar mass and density
options.explanation: None of these is an equilibrium lever.

options.text: Surface area, light and pH for all equilibria
options.explanation: Not the trio named by the principle here.

check.stem: Adding a catalyst to an equilibrium mixture will

options.text: Leave the position of equilibrium unchanged
options.explanation: Catalysts speed both directions equally, so the balance never moves.

options.text: Shift the position to the right
options.explanation: No shift results from catalysis.

options.text: Shift the position to the left
options.explanation: No shift results from catalysis.

options.text: Raise the equilibrium constant
options.explanation: The constant depends on temperature alone.

check.stem: State Le Chatelier's principle.
check.modelAnswer: A disturbance to any system at dynamic equilibrium makes the position of equilibrium shift so as to counteract the disturbance.

check.stem: State what a shift to the left does to reactant concentration.
check.modelAnswer: A leftward shift increases the concentration of the reactants.

check.stem: Explain why the counteraction of Le Chatelier's principle is only partial.
check.modelAnswer: The shift reduces the imposed disturbance by moving composition, but the new equilibrium still differs from the original, so the change is softened rather than erased.

check.stem: An equilibrium mixture is suddenly compressed. State the principle's prediction and identify which direction of shift would reduce the pressure.
check.modelAnswer: The position shifts toward the side with fewer gas moles, reducing total gas count and so softening the pressure rise - that is the counteracting direction.

lessons.title: Concentration levers on the equilibrium position
lessons.opening: Feed the reactants or drain the products and the equilibrium rewards you: adding reactant or removing product both push the position rightward, lifting yield. The esterification mixture shows the arithmetic of each disturbance.
keyPoints: Increasing reactant concentration shifts the position right, using up the excess and forming more products.
Decreasing reactant concentration shifts left to replace the lost reactant, consuming products.
Increasing product concentration shifts left; decreasing product concentration shifts right, boosting yield.
To maximise yield, raise reactant concentration or remove products as they form.

low.restatement: Add reactant: rightward shift eats the excess. Remove reactant: leftward shift rebuilds it. The same mirror logic runs for products, and industrial chemists exploit the product-removal case.
low.analogy: A shop restocks whatever gets bought: clear the shelves (products) and the supplier (forward reaction) restocks harder.
low.examPointer: Quote the yield rule - increase reactant concentration or continuously remove products - when asked how to push an equilibrium rightward.

medium.restatement: Each disturbance forces a temporary rate imbalance: adding reactant spikes the forward rate, so composition drifts right until rates re-equalise. The counteraction never restores the original concentrations exactly.
medium.analogy: Overfilling one end of a balanced tank sends water flowing toward the other end until levels settle somewhere new.
medium.examPointer: In the esterification example, adding ethyl ethanoate (a product) shifts the position left - recognising product species matters more than their name.

check.stem: Increasing the concentration of a reactant shifts the position of equilibrium

options.text: To the right, using up the excess reactant to form more products
options.explanation: The system counteracts the addition by consuming it.

options.text: To the left, replacing the lost reactant
options.explanation: Nothing was lost; it was added.

options.text: Nowhere, as concentration cannot shift equilibria
options.explanation: Concentration is one of the three shifting variables.

options.text: Randomly, depending on the catalyst
options.explanation: Catalysts play no role in position.

check.stem: Some ethanol is removed from the esterification equilibrium CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> ester + water. The position

options.text: Shifts left, producing more ethanoic acid and ethanol from the ester side
options.explanation: Removing a reactant triggers replacement of the loss, consuming products.

options.text: Shifts right, forming more ester
options.explanation: Removal of a reactant cannot favour the product side.

options.text: Stays put because alcohols are inert
options.explanation: Ethanol is a reacting species here.

options.text: Shifts right and doubles the water formed
options.explanation: No doubling rule exists in Le Chatelier reasoning.

check.stem: Adding more ethyl ethanoate (the ester product) to the equilibrium mixture shifts the position

options.text: Left, to use up the excess product and restore ethanoic acid and ethanol
options.explanation: The system counteracts product addition by consuming it.

options.text: Right, making even more ester
options.explanation: That would amplify the disturbance, against the principle.

options.text: Nowhere, because products cannot shift equilibria
options.explanation: Product concentration is a genuine lever.

options.text: Left and permanently doubling the acid
options.explanation: Counteraction is partial, never a doubling.

check.stem: Adding water to the Ce4+ + Fe2+ equilibrium mixture has what effect?

options.text: No effect, as water dilutes all ions equally without changing the balance
options.explanation: Uniform dilution leaves the reactant-to-product ratio untouched.

options.text: A rightward shift, because more liquid is present
options.explanation: Dilution is not a composition change of the reacting ions.

options.text: A leftward shift, because water is a product
options.explanation: Water is not part of this ionic equilibrium.

options.text: It stops the reaction entirely
options.explanation: Diluted ions still react.

check.stem: To increase the yield of an equilibrium product, an industrial chemist should

options.text: Increase reactant concentration or remove products as they form
options.explanation: Both disturbances push the position toward products.

options.text: Decrease reactant concentration
options.explanation: That pushes the position leftward.

options.text: Add a catalyst
options.explanation: Catalysts change rate, not yield.

options.text: Increase product concentration
options.explanation: That pushes the position leftward too.

check.stem: State the effect of decreasing the concentration of a product at equilibrium.
check.modelAnswer: The position shifts right to replace the lost product, increasing the yield.

check.stem: State the two yield-maximising concentration strategies.
check.modelAnswer: Increase the concentration of reactants, or continuously remove the products as they form.

check.stem: Explain why removing a product shifts the position of equilibrium to the right.
check.modelAnswer: The backward rate depends on product concentration; removing product slows the backward reaction below the forward rate, so composition drifts rightward until the rates re-equalise.

check.stem: An ethyl ethanoate producer wants more ester per batch. Give two Le Chatelier actions on the equilibrium CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O.
check.modelAnswer: Use excess ethanoic acid or ethanol (raising reactant concentration), and continuously remove the water or ester formed (lowering product concentration), both driving the position rightward.

lessons.title: Pressure levers and the gas-mole census
lessons.opening: Pressure only speaks to gases: squeeze an equilibrium and it retreats toward whichever side holds fewer gas moles. Count the molecules, pick the side - and when the counts tie, nothing moves at all.
keyPoints: Pressure changes affect only equilibria with gaseous reactants or products.
Increasing pressure shifts the position toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
Decreasing pressure shifts toward the side with more moles of gas.
With matching gas-mole totals on the two sides, pressure shifts nothing.

low.restatement: Count gas moles left and right: the higher-pressure side loses. Solids and liquids carry no vote; equal gas counts mean no response at all.
low.analogy: A crowded bus sheds passengers toward the emptier carriage when squeezed - gases do the same, retreating to the less crowded side.
low.examPointer: Count only gaseous species; solids like CaCO3 and CaO contribute zero to the census.

medium.restatement: Raising pressure raises collision frequency per volume; the system offsets the squeeze by shifting to the lower-mole side, reducing total gas count. Equal counts give no directional preference, so no shift occurs.
medium.analogy: Squeezing a balloon with unequal pockets: air migrates to the roomier side.
medium.examPointer: For CaCO3 <=> CaO + CO2, the left side has zero gas moles - compression pushes leftward against the carbon dioxide.

check.stem: Increasing the pressure on N2O4 (g) <=> 2NO2 (g) shifts the position

options.text: To the left, toward the single mole of gas on the N2O4 side
options.explanation: Fewer gas moles relieves the imposed pressure rise.

options.text: To the right, toward the two moles of NO2
options.explanation: More moles would raise pressure further, amplifying the change.

options.text: Nowhere, as both sides are gaseous
options.explanation: Unequal gas counts always respond to pressure.

options.text: To the left only if a catalyst is present
options.explanation: Catalysts are irrelevant to position.

check.stem: For CaCO3 (s) <=> CaO (s) + CO2 (g), increasing pressure shifts the position

options.text: To the left, because only CO2 counts as gas: zero versus one mole
options.explanation: Solids are excluded from the census, leaving 0 left vs 1 right.

options.text: To the right, because the solid takes up space
options.explanation: Solids and liquids do not enter the gas-mole count.

options.text: Nowhere, as no gases react
options.explanation: CO2 is a gas and participates.

options.text: To the left and stops the decomposition
options.explanation: The shift reduces, not stops, decomposition.

check.stem: Decreasing the pressure on 2NO2 (g) <=> 2NO (g) + O2 (g) shifts the position

options.text: To the right, toward the three moles of gas
options.explanation: Lower pressure is relieved by occupying more volume with more moles.

options.text: To the left, toward the two moles
options.explanation: Fewer moles suits higher pressure, not lower.

options.text: Nowhere, since moles are close
options.explanation: 2 versus 3 is unequal, so a shift occurs.

options.text: To the right only at high temperature
options.explanation: Temperature and pressure shifts are separate levers.

check.stem: When gas moles are equal on both sides, increasing pressure

options.text: Has no effect on the position of equilibrium
options.explanation: No side is favoured, so no shift occurs.

options.text: Shifts the position right
options.explanation: No directional preference exists.

options.text: Shifts the position left
options.explanation: No directional preference exists.

options.text: Raises the equilibrium constant
options.explanation: Constants respond to temperature only.

check.stem: Why do solids and liquids not affect pressure shifts?

options.text: Their volumes barely change under pressure, unlike compressible gases
options.explanation: The pressure lever operates through gas volume compression.

options.text: They are always in excess
options.explanation: Amount has no bearing on the census rule.

options.text: They cannot change oxidation states
options.explanation: Redox is unrelated to pressure shifts.

options.text: They evaporate instantly under pressure
options.explanation: Nothing of the sort happens.

check.stem: State the direction of shift when pressure is increased on an equilibrium.
check.modelAnswer: Toward the side with fewer moles of gas.

check.stem: State the condition in which pressure changes leave an equilibrium unmoved.
check.modelAnswer: When the gas-mole totals match on the two sides of the equation.

check.stem: Explain why pressure changes do not affect equilibria without gases.
check.modelAnswer: Pressure acts through the compressibility of gases; with no gaseous species present, there is no volume response for the system to counteract.

check.stem: A chemist doubles the pressure on H2 (g) + I2 (g) <=> 2HI (g). Predict and justify the shift.
check.modelAnswer: No shift: both sides carry two gas moles, so the pressure change has no directional preference despite every species being gaseous.

lessons.title: Temperature levers and the endothermic compass
lessons.opening: Temperature shifts ride the sign of the enthalpy change: heating pushes equilibrium in the endothermic direction, cooling in the exothermic. The hydrogen-carbon dioxide mixture with its +41.2 kJ mol-1 forward change gives the rule a number to bite on.
keyPoints: Raising the temperature drives the equilibrium toward the endothermic side, absorbing the extra heat.
Decreasing temperature shifts the position in the exothermic direction.
For H2 + CO2 <=> H2O + CO with forward ΔH = +41.2 kJ mol-1, heating shifts the position right.
If heating increases a product, the forward reaction is endothermic by Le Chatelier's principle.

low.restatement: Heat is a product of exothermic directions and a reactant of endothermic ones; treat added heat like added reactant and the shift direction follows mechanically.
low.analogy: A see-saw where heat is a weight: dump heat on the exothermic side and the balance tips toward the endothermic side to absorb it.
low.examPointer: Deduce enthalpy sign from observations too: if warming raises a product, the forward reaction absorbs heat - it is endothermic.

medium.restatement: The temperature lever uniquely alters the equilibrium constant itself, unlike concentration and pressure which only shift position. The endothermic direction consumes imposed heat; the exothermic direction releases it, restoring balance.
medium.analogy: Two banks of a river trading heat like currency: warming hands more heat to the bank that spends it (endothermic).
medium.examPointer: State explicitly that only temperature changes K - a favourite discrimination question against the other two levers.

check.stem: Increasing the temperature of an equilibrium shifts the position

options.text: In the endothermic direction
options.explanation: The system absorbs the imposed heat by favouring the heat-consuming direction.

options.text: In the exothermic direction
options.explanation: That is the response to cooling.

options.text: Nowhere, as temperature only changes rate
options.explanation: Temperature also shifts position and changes the constant.

options.text: Toward the side with fewer gas moles
options.explanation: That is the pressure rule.

check.stem: For H2 + CO2 <=> H2O + CO (forward ΔH = +41.2 kJ mol-1), heating shifts the position

options.text: To the right, the endothermic forward direction, to absorb the extra energy
options.explanation: The positive ΔH marks the forward reaction as heat-consuming.

options.text: To the left, the exothermic direction
options.explanation: Leftward is the backward reaction, which is exothermic - heating favours the other direction.

options.text: Nowhere, as ΔH is small
options.explanation: The sign, not the size, sets the direction.

options.text: To the right and doubles the constant
options.explanation: No doubling rule exists.

check.stem: Cooling an equilibrium mixture shifts the position in the exothermic direction because

options.text: The system replaces lost heat by favouring the heat-releasing direction
options.explanation: The exothermic direction supplies the energy withdrawn by cooling.

options.text: Cold always favours products
options.explanation: Direction depends on the enthalpy sign, not a universal product rule.

options.text: Rates stop changing when cooled
options.explanation: Rates fall, but the position also shifts.

options.text: The equilibrium constant is unchanged by temperature
options.explanation: Temperature uniquely changes the constant.

check.stem: Heating Ag2CO3 (s) <=> Ag2O (s) + CO2 (g) increases CO2 at constant pressure. The forward reaction is

options.text: Endothermic, since heating drives the heat-consuming forward direction
options.explanation: More CO2 on heating means the forward reaction absorbs heat.

options.text: Exothermic, since heat is produced
options.explanation: Heat production would be suppressed by heating, lowering CO2.

options.text: Neither, as solids dominate
options.explanation: The CO2 signal is measurable regardless of the solids.

options.text: Impossible to deduce
options.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle deduces it directly.

check.stem: Which lever changes the value of the equilibrium constant?

options.text: Temperature only
options.explanation: Concentration and pressure shift position without touching the constant.

options.text: Concentration
options.explanation: Shifts position; the constant stays fixed.

options.text: Pressure
options.explanation: Shifts position; the constant stays fixed.

options.text: A catalyst
options.explanation: Changes neither position nor constant.

check.stem: State the direction of shift when temperature is decreased.
check.modelAnswer: The position shifts in the exothermic direction.

check.stem: State the temperature shift for a reaction whose forward change is endothermic.
check.modelAnswer: Increasing temperature shifts the position toward the products (rightward), the endothermic direction.

check.stem: Explain why heating favours the endothermic direction.
check.modelAnswer: The imposed temperature rise is a disturbance; the system counteracts it by absorbing heat, which only the endothermic direction can do.

check.stem: For an equilibrium whose forward reaction is exothermic, predict the two shift directions for heating and cooling.
check.modelAnswer: Heating shifts the position left (the endothermic backward direction), reducing product yield; cooling shifts it right (exothermic forward), raising yield.

glossary.definition: The balance between product amounts and reactant amounts held in an equilibrium mixture.
The rule that a system at equilibrium shifts to counteract any imposed change.
The reaction direction that absorbs heat; favoured by increasing temperature.

workedExample.prompt: Pressure on the equilibrium N2O4 (g) <=> 2NO2 (g) is raised. Predict the shift.
steps: Count gas moles on each side: 1 mole of N2O4 on the left versus 2 moles of NO2 on the right.
Apply the census rule: increasing pressure shifts toward the side with fewer gas moles.
The left side (1 mole) is the fewer-mole side, so the position moves left, reducing total gas count and softening the pressure rise.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The equilibrium shifts to the left (toward N2O4).
